claims.statement: Distributed systems need not expose one directly observable global time.
Send/source order can differ from receive order under unequal transport delays.
Causal precedence can be represented as a partial order and logical clocks can represent constraints consistent with that order.
A concrete serialization can be a topological ordering of a dependency graph without being identical to that graph.
Causal consistency preserves causally related operation order while permitting flexibility for concurrent operations under the system model.
Logical or process-local ordering coordinates are not automatically relativistic proper time.
claims.scope: distinction between distributed-systems logical time and physical proper time

claims.statement: A transport acknowledgement does not by itself establish execution, observation, or acknowledgement of the intended application effect.
Later-arriving evidence can refine a provenance-constrained reconstructed event history without implying physical backward-time transport.
The QIK-VRT universal grammar of understanding is a project-specific research interpretation and is not established scientific consensus.
The article does not claim a physical time machine, reception before emission, backward-running relativistic proper time, or controllable signalling into one's own causal past.
